Let me carefully grade this write-up.

The problem: sequence defined greedily; prove eventually (actually globally from n=1) translation-periodic: a_{n+T} = a_n + L.

The grading rubric:
- "answer": the claimed structure (L a product of finitely many small primes, T a count of residues) is stated (2 correct and explicit, 1 vague, 0 absent/wrong).
- "reduction" = (C): characterization that an integer m >= a_1 is a term iff its prime support meets the prime support of every term (equivalently of every earlier term).
- "lower_bound" = (F): finiteness / large-prime erasure lemma — membership depends only on primes in some finite set, because any term divisible by a large prime is dominated by a smaller number with the same small-prime support that is itself a term — proved for ALL terms, not on examples.
- "upper_bound" = (P): global periodicity from n=1: with L = product of relevant primes, membership invariant under m -> m+L for every m >= a_1, and T count of terms in a window of length L, giving a_{n+T} = a_n + L for all n >= 1.

Now let me analyze the write-up.

The write-up:

1. Reinterprets the construction as a greedy scan: an integer >= a_1 is accepted iff it is noncoprime to every earlier accepted integer. Actually careful: they claim "accepting an integer if and only if it has gcd > 1 with every integer accepted earlier. The accepted integers, in increasing order, are exactly a_1, a_2, ...". This is the standard characterization. They prove it: "Indeed, this is precisely the minimality condition in the definition of a_{n+1}." Hmm, this is a bit brief, but it's essentially right: the definition says a_{n+1} is the smallest integer > a_n that is noncoprime to all a_i, i <= n. The greedy scan equivalence: standard argument that the greedy scan accepted set equals the sequence. The claim that this is "precisely the minimality condition" is a bit terse but acceptable as a correct reduction. Let me consider: this is mechanism (C) — the characterization that m >= a_1 is a term iff its prime support meets the support of every term (equivalently, every earlier term). The write-up proves:

- Claim: acceptance depends only on support among integers >= a_1. Proof: if x rejected, there's a smaller accepted witness coprime to x; same support implies witness coprime to y, so y rejected. If x accepted, every accepted integer smaller than y is noncoprime to x... wait, they use "accepted integers are pairwise noncoprime" to say every accepted integer smaller than y is noncoprime to x (since x accepted, pairwise noncoprime with all accepted). Then y shares support with x so y noncoprime with every accepted integer smaller than y, so y is accepted. Good.

- Self-duality (1): S in F iff S meets every member of F. Forward: accepted integers pairwise noncoprime. Converse: if S meets every member of F, choose integer x >= a_1 with support S; every accepted integer smaller than x has support in F, hence noncoprime to x; hence x accepted. Good — this is the characterization (C).

So "reduction" = (C) is fully written out. Score 2.

Wait — one subtlety in the converse of (1): they need that every accepted integer smaller than x has support in F. F is defined as the family of supports whose integers of sufficiently large size are accepted. Since support-determined acceptance was proven, membership in F is well-defined for each support. Accepted integers smaller than x have supports in F (since acceptance is support-determined). Then S meets each such support, so x noncoprime to all earlier accepted. Then greedy scan accepts x. Fine.

Actually, there's a subtle point: the proof of "acceptance depends only on support" uses "every rejected integer x > a_1 has a smaller accepted integer coprime to it" — which follows from the greedy scan characterization. And the greedy scan characterization itself needs a small argument: the accepted integers by scan are a_1, a_2, ... Let me verify: by induction, suppose the first n accepted are a_1..a_n. The next accepted by the scan is the smallest integer > a_n noncoprime to all of a_1..a_n, which is exactly a_{n+1} by definition. Yes, that's fine. The write-up says "Indeed, this is precisely the minimality condition in the definition of a_{n+1}." That's essentially the induction. OK.

So (C): 2.

2. (F): finiteness / large-prime erasure. The rubric says: "membership depends only on the primes in some finite set (e.g. primes <= a_1 or <= a_1^2), because any term divisible by a large prime is dominated by a smaller number with the same small-prime support that is itself a term -- proved for ALL terms, not checked on examples."

The write-up proves finiteness differently: via minimal supports C, Lemma 1 (bounded-size finiteness via infinite sunflower + self-duality), Lemma 2 (weight descent: if C in C and p in C, then there's D in C containing p with w(D \ {p}) < a_1). This shows every prime occurring in a minimal support occurs in a "terminal" member, which has bounded size (<= log2 a_1 + 1), and by Lemma 1 only finitely many such terminal members, so P finite, so C finite (all subsets of finite P). Then membership depends only on primes in P (finite set), hence periodic mod L = product of P.

This is indeed a finiteness proof: the set of primes that matter is finite, and membership is determined by support intersected with P (in fact, containment of some C in C, where C ⊆ P). This is analogous to (F): "membership depends only on the primes in some finite set." The mechanism is different from the "large-prime erasure" sketched in the rubric, but the rubric says "the FINITENESS / large-prime-erasure lemma: membership depends only on the primes in some finite set (e.g. primes <= a_1 or <= a_1^2), because any term divisible by a large prime is dominated by a smaller number with the same small-prime support that is itself a term". Hmm. The rubric gives an example mechanism, but the core is the finiteness lemma. Let me check whether the write-up's finiteness argument is correct and complete for all cases.

Let me scrutinize Lemma 2's descent step carefully.

Descent step: E ∈ C, p ∈ E, w(E \ {p}) >= a_1. S = E \ {p}. By inclusion-minimality of E, S ∉ F. The squarefree integer w(S) has support S, is >= a_1, and is therefore rejected. Hence there exists an accepted integer y < w(S) coprime to w(S). The support of y lies in F, so it contains some H ∈ C.

Check: S ∉ F because E is inclusion-minimal in F and S ⊊ E. Yes, since S ⊆ E, S ≠ E (p ∈ E \ S), so minimality gives S ∉ F. Since acceptance depends only on support (for integers >= a_1), and w(S) >= a_1 has support S ∉ F, w(S) is rejected. Rejected means there's a smaller accepted integer coprime to it (from the greedy scan property: every rejected integer x > a_1 has a smaller accepted coprime witness). Note: w(S) >= a_1 and rejected — is w(S) > a_1? If w(S) = a_1, then it would be accepted since a_1 is accepted (a_1 is accepted as the first term; its support is in F). Since w(S) is rejected, w(S) ≠ a_1... hmm, actually if w(S) = a_1 then supp(a_1) = S ∈ F, contradiction. So w(S) > a_1 and rejected, so there's y < w(S) accepted with gcd(y, w(S)) = 1. Actually the greedy scan property gives y accepted with y < w(S) (since w(S) rejected, at the time of scanning w(S) some earlier accepted integer is coprime to it; that accepted integer is < w(S)). Wait, the write-up established "every rejected integer x > a_1 has a smaller accepted integer coprime to it." But actually the correct statement is: there's a smaller accepted integer coprime to it. Yes, since the scan rejects x because some earlier accepted integer is coprime to it. Good.

Then H ∈ C with H ⊆ supp(y). H ∩ S = ∅ since supp(y) ∩ S = ∅ (coprimality). H ∩ E ≠ ∅ (intersecting). E = S ∪ {p}, so p ∈ H. Also w(H) ≤ prod_{q | y} q = w(supp(y)) ≤ y < w(S). Indeed w(H) ≤ w(supp(y)) ≤ y since y >= product of its distinct primes. Good.

So descent step: from E (with p ∈ E and w(E\{p}) >= a_1) to H ∈ C with p ∈ H and w(H) < w(E \ {p}).

Repeated descent: starting from C, as long as current E satisfies w(E \ {p}) >= a_1, replace E by H. Each H contains p. Weights strictly decrease: w(H) < w(E \ {p}) < w(E) (since w(E) = w(E\{p}) · p ≥ 2 w(E\{p}) > w(E\{p}) > w(H)). Actually need w(H) < w(E\{p}) to be a decreasing measure; they say "(5) shows that its weight is strictly smaller than the weight of the preceding member." w(H) < w(E \ {p}) ≤ w(E)/2 < w(E). Yes strictly decreasing positive integers, so terminates. At termination, D ∈ C contains p and w(D \ {p}) < a_1. Lemma 2 correct.

Wait — subtlety: the descent step requires w(E \ {p}) >= a_1 to run. The termination condition: we stop when w(E \ {p}) < a_1. The output D satisfies (4). Good.

Terminal members: D with w(D \ {p}) < a_1 for some p ∈ D. Then 2^{|D|-1} ≤ w(D\{p}) < a_1... hmm, 2^{|D|-1} ≤ w(D \ {p}) requires |D \ {p}| = |D| - 1 and all primes ≥ 2, so w(D\{p}) ≥ 2^{|D|-1}. So |D| ≤ 1 + log2(a_1 - 1) < a_1 for a_1 > 2... For a_1 = 2: 2^{|D|-1} < 2, so |D| - 1 ≤ 0, |D| ≤ 1. Fine. They say |D| ≤ a_1. Hmm, 2^{|D|-1} < a_1 implies |D| - 1 < log2 a_1 ≤ a_1 - 1 for a_1 ≥ 2? For a_1 = 2: log2 2 = 1, |D| ≤ 2 - 1 = 1. In general 2^{k-1} < a_1 gives k - 1 ≤ ceil(log2 a_1) - 1, i.e., k ≤ ceil(log2 a_1). And ceil(log2 a_1) ≤ a_1 for a_1 ≥ 1. Yes |D| ≤ a_1. Fine (with K = a_1 in Lemma 1).

Lemma 1: For every K, only finitely many C ∈ C with |C| ≤ K. Proof via infinite sunflower: an infinite family of distinct sets of size ≤ K contains an infinite subfamily with pairwise intersections equal to fixed R. The "elementary infinite sunflower fact": They claim every infinite family of distinct sets of size at most K has an infinite subfamily C_1, C_2, ... with C_i ∩ C_j = R for i ≠ j. Hmm — this is the Δ-system (sunflower) lemma for infinite families, which is easier than the finite version: induction on K. If some element occurs in infinitely many sets, restrict to those sets, delete the element, apply induction to get a Δ-system R' among the deleted sets; then R = R' ∪ {element} — wait, need care: the infinite subfamily of sets containing element x, delete x from each, get infinite family of sets of size ≤ K-1, by induction get infinite subfamily with pairwise intersection R'; then original sets have pairwise intersection R' ∪ {x}. Yes. If every element occurs only finitely often, greedily pick pairwise disjoint sets: pick any set S_1, its elements each occur finitely often, so only finitely many sets intersect S_1; remove them, pick S_2 disjoint from S_1 among remaining, etc. Infinite. R = ∅. This is correct. The write-up sketches this: "For completeness, this fact follows by induction on K. If some element occurs in infinitely many sets, restrict to those sets, delete that element, and apply the induction hypothesis. If every element occurs only finitely many times, one can greedily choose infinitely many pairwise disjoint sets, giving R = ∅." That's a complete sketch; the induction is valid. OK.

Then: petals C_i \ R pairwise disjoint. Fix any H ∈ C. C is intersecting, so H meets every C_i, i.e., H ∩ C_i ≠ ∅. If H ∩ R = ∅, then H meets C_i \ R for every i; petals pairwise disjoint, H finite → impossible. So every H ∈ C meets R. Wait — "Thus every H ∈ C meets R." Careful: the argument shows for each H ∈ C, H ∩ R ≠ ∅. Yes.

Then every member of F contains a member of C, so R meets every member of F (R meets every member of C, and every F-member contains a C-member... wait: if F ∋ S ⊇ C' for some C' ∈ C, then R ∩ C' ≠ ∅ so R ∩ S ≠ ∅). OK so H_0 ⊆ R ⊆ C_i, antichain forces H_0 = C_i for all i, contradicting distinctness (there are infinitely many distinct C_i). Correct.

Hmm wait, one more check: R ∈ F requires R nonempty (F is family of nonempty finite prime sets). R meets every H ∈ C and C is nonempty (contains supp(a_1)'s minimal subset... actually supp(a_1) ∈ F, so C nonempty). So R ≠ ∅. Good. Also, R is a finite set of primes, and by (1) R ∈ F. Fine.

Then P = union of terminal members, finite. Every prime in any C ∈ C is in some terminal D by Lemma 2. So C ⊆ 2^P, C finite. Good.

So the finiteness (F-analogue) is fully proven for all cases: the set of "relevant" primes is P = union of terminal minimal supports, finite. Membership of m ≥ a_1 depends only on supp(m) ∩ P? The idea that large primes get "erased" because the squarefree kernel w(S) ≥ a_1 being rejected yields a smaller witness... It's a legitimate, fully general finiteness proof.
